meta.topic: Failure and timeout across corridor legs

problem:
Meridian Bank, a fictional bank, runs an instant cross-border corridor where the payment crosses two fast payment systems joined by an orchestration layer. A customer sends money, the app times out, and the customer taps send again. The bank now has two instructions, one debit, no destination confirmation, and a customer who does not know whether the money has gone.

The failure is not a single broken step. It is an uncertain outcome spread across corridor legs: the originating leg may have been accepted, the destination leg may have succeeded late, the response may have been lost, or the payment may never have left. Each possibility needs a different response, and the wrong response, a blind resubmission or a premature refund, creates a duplicate payment or a double compensation.

The bank must handle uncertain outcome, status enquiry, no duplicate retry and inter PSP investigation as one disciplined process, so every timeout ends in a known outcome with exactly one financial effect.
solution:
Treat every timeout as an unknown outcome, never as an automatic failure and never as an automatic success. The channel must show a pending or unknown status, not a failure, and the payment engine must hold the payment in an unknown state until an authoritative event resolves it. That discipline is what stops a customer retry from becoming a duplicate payment.

Resolve the unknown by enquiry, not by resubmission. The payment engine queries the orchestration layer, the destination rail and the ledger by correlation ID and, where applicable, by UETR, and compares the leg states. A retry from the channel must carry the same idempotency key as the original instruction, so the engine recognises it as the same payment and returns the current known state instead of creating a new transaction. Only when the enquiry proves the original payment did not execute may a new instruction be created, and it carries a new idempotency key.

Model each corridor leg separately with an overall orchestration state. The originating leg, the settlement leg and the destination leg each have their own state machine, timeout and confirmation rule, and the overall state is unknown until the required leg confirmations have arrived or the timeout has triggered investigation. A late success after a timeout is a known race: the late event is applied to the original payment, and any refund already issued is reversed or reconciled under the defined process, so the outcome is never both a beneficiary credit and a sender refund.

Give the unknown state a governed investigation path. At the defined timeout the payment moves to an inter PSP investigation with a named owner, a service level and a customer communication plan. The investigation uses status enquiry, tracker events and ledger evidence, and it closes only when the outcome is proven: settled, rejected, returned or compensated, each with its own linked accounting event.

decision.question: A customer submits an instant cross-border payment, the channel times out with no response, and the customer retries with a new instruction. The payment engine shows one accepted payment and one duplicate instruction. What should the bank do?

options.label: A
options.detail: Treat the timeout as an unknown outcome, enquire by the original correlation ID, deduplicate the retry with the same idempotency key, and resolve the original payment before creating any new financial effect.

options.label: B
options.detail: Refund the customer immediately and also send the payment, to be safe.

options.label: C
options.detail: Execute both instructions, since the customer sent both.

options.label: D
options.detail: Cancel both and tell the customer to start again tomorrow.

decisionRationale: Option A is correct because a timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure, and it must be resolved by enquiry and deduplication before any new posting. Option C is wrong because it can duplicate the payment. Option D is wrong because it discards a payment that may already have settled. Option B is wrong because it can both credit the beneficiary and refund the sender.

steps.title: Submits an instant cross-border payment in the channel
Assigns a correlation ID and an idempotency key and records the instruction
Debits the sender where the product design requires it and initiates the originating leg
Forwards the payment through the settlement arrangement to the destination rail
Times out waiting for a response and shows the customer a pending or unknown status
Runs a status enquiry by correlation ID across the legs and the ledger
Investigates the unknown outcome with the destination participant where the enquiry cannot resolve it
Applies the proven outcome once, posts the linked accounting, and tells the customer the final result

happy: The customer submits a payment, the originating leg is accepted, the orchestration settles it, the destination leg credits the beneficiary, the confirmation arrives within the timeout, the ledger posts once, and the customer sees a confirmed completion with the reference.

negative.title: Timeout after submission with unknown outcome
negative.detail: The channel times out and it is unclear whether the engine accepted or executed the payment. Treat the outcome as unknown, enquire by correlation ID, expose a pending or unknown state, and retry only with the same idempotency key.

negative.title: Late success after timeout
negative.detail: A destination success arrives after the timeout and after a refund was considered. Apply the late event to the original payment and resolve it without both crediting the beneficiary and refunding the sender.

negative.title: Duplicate retry
negative.detail: The customer retries the same payment with a new instruction. Deduplicate by idempotency key, return the current known state, and create no new financial effect.

negative.title: Return and success race
negative.detail: A return and a success event arrive for the same payment in either order. Apply event ordering and the leg state machine, hold the payment for investigation where the race cannot be resolved safely, and post only the proven outcome.

technical: Use a durable payment record with a correlation ID, an idempotency key and, where applicable, a UETR, and persist the state of each leg separately with timestamps and event versions. Make every consumer idempotent with persisted inbound message IDs and processed outcomes, and enforce a state machine that prevents regression and duplicate posting. Use outbox and inbox patterns so a status event is never lost between systems, and provide a status enquiry API that returns the current known state by reference without creating a transaction. Log every enquiry, retry, timeout and investigation event as structured audit data, and reconcile the status store against the ledger and the clearing acknowledgements intraday.

messages.title: Customer payment initiation carrying the idempotency key and references
Customer credit transfer for the payment leg
Payment status report resolving the leg outcome
Payment return where a settled payment must be returned
Cancellation request only where a valid cancellation process is initiated, with acceptance not guaranteed

accounting: A payment in an unknown state holds its funds in suspense with a linked investigation case, and no second posting is made until the outcome is proven. A proven success posts the beneficiary credit and settlement entries once; a proven failure releases the reservation once and restores the sender balance; a proven return posts as a linked pacs.004 event, never by editing the original debit. A late success that arrives after a refund triggers a reconciliation case to recover the duplicate effect under the defined process. Operations monitor timeout rates, unknown state ageing, duplicate retry rates and investigation resolution times as corridor quality measures, with ageing alerts so no unknown payment sits unresolved.

scenarios.when: the client enquires using the original reference
scenarios.then: the platform returns the current known state. does not create a new transaction

scenarios.given: a timeout followed by a late success
scenarios.then: the system resolves the transaction without both crediting the beneficiary and refunding the sender. the investigation case is closed with the proven outcome

questions.question: What does a submission timeout mean?
options: The outcome is unknown until an enquiry resolves it
questions.explanation: A timeout means the outcome is unknown, not a failure or a success.

questions.question: How should a retry after a timeout be sent?
options: With the same idempotency key as the original instruction
As a completely new payment with a different amount
With a new idempotency key every time
questions.explanation: A retry must reuse the same idempotency key so it is recognised as the same payment.

questions.question: What must not happen when a late success arrives after a timeout?
options: Both crediting the beneficiary and refunding the sender
The late event is applied to the original payment
The customer is told the final outcome
questions.explanation: Exactly one financial effect must occur, so a late success must not combine with a refund.

questions.question: When may camt.056 be used?
options: Only where a valid cancellation process is initiated, with acceptance not guaranteed
To cancel any payment at any time with guaranteed acceptance
questions.explanation: Cancellation via camt.056 is a request process, and acceptance is not guaranteed.
